system:
You are a computational cancer biologist searching CRISPR screen data for selective genetic dependencies: genes that cancer cells with a particular alteration (the biomarker) need more than other cancer cells do. Such genes are candidate drug targets with a built-in patient-selection strategy.

Work like a careful scientist:
1. Plan first with write_plan, and revise it as you learn.
2. Survey the data (genome_wide_top, scan_biomarker, scan_target) to generate candidate hypotheses.
3. Be sceptical before you believe a signal. Use inspect_association to check whether it is driven by one lineage or a disease subtype hiding inside a lineage, and whether the effect is large enough to matter. Ask whether the biology makes sense (paralog buffering, pathway dependence, oncogene addiction). A broadly essential target may lack a therapeutic window.
4. Check the literature with search_pubmed before registering, and judge novelty honestly.
5. Register only your best hypotheses (register_hypothesis). Registration is final and must come before replication. You have 5 replications, each of which must pass one-sided p < 0.01 in BOTH held-out Broad cell lines and independent Sanger screens.
6. Report honestly with submit_findings. A hypothesis is replicated only if replicate() said so. Negative results are results. Never let what you remember from the literature override what the data show.

You have at most 15 model turns. Batch independent tool calls in one turn.
task_prompt:
Patient population of interest: cancers with biomarker HOT_PIK3CA (PIK3CA hotspot mutation).

Find the single best candidate therapeutic target for this population: the gene these cell lines depend on most selectively, supported by the data. Register your top candidate (you may register up to two), replicate it, and submit findings with your best candidate listed first.

I'll run a quick scan on PIK3CA and a PubMed search to confirm, then register and replicate it. I might also look at the genome-wide top list for other PI3K pathway candidates, keeping the number of turns low.

input.mechanism: Hotspot-activated PI3K p110alpha drives PI3K/AKT signaling; mutant lines become addicted to the mutant catalytic subunit (oncogene addiction), so PIK3CA knockout is more lethal in HOT_PIK3CA lines than in other lines, across lineages.

name: register_hypothesis

input.mechanism: Hotspot-activated PI3K p110alpha drives PI3K/AKT signaling; mutant lines become addicted to the mutant catalytic subunit (oncogene addiction), so PIK3CA knockout is more lethal in HOT_PIK3CA lines than in other lines, across lineages.

output: Registered H1_PIK3CA_hotspot_to_PIK3CA: HOT_PIK3CA -> more dependent on PIK3CA. Discovery evidence frozen: t=-12.98, n_altered=62. Replication budget left: 5. Replication passes only if one-sided p < 0.01 in BOTH held-out Broad lines and Sanger screens.

findings.claim: PIK3CA hotspot-mutant lines are selectively dependent on PIK3CA (lineage-adjusted beta -0.54, 51/62 altered lines strongly dependent vs 180/564 others); replicated in held-out Broad lines (beta -0.41, p=4e-13) and independent Sanger screen (beta -0.67, p=3e-24).

input.summary: Top candidate for HOT_PIK3CA cancers is PIK3CA itself. Across 626 discovery lines (62 altered), PIK3CA is the strongest and only highly significant selective dependency (q=7e-30; 82% of altered lines dependent vs. mean effect -0.93 vs -0.41 in others). The effect holds within breast, endometrial, bladder, ovarian, and gastric lineages, is not driven by expression differences, and replicated in held-out Broad lines and an independent Sanger screen. Other associated genes (SERPINH1, ARHGAP4, FOXA1, AKT1) were not significant after FDR correction, and the AKT1 signal was weak. The dependency is on-target and well known clinically (mutant PI3Kα inhibitors such as alpelisib and inavolisib), so novelty is low, but it validates the approach. The main limitation is that PIK3CA is a known target, not a new one.
